newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dividend tax change discussions planned.
newsitem.headline: Australian dividend tax change discussions planned.

text.p: Australian government officials have agreed to meet funds management industry leaders again to thrash out controversial changes to dividend taxation rules.
The meeting will be held in Canberra within two weeks, to be hosted by the Treasury Department and Australian Tax Office, industry and government sources told Reuters.

Some industry leaders said the willingness of the bureaucrats to continue listening to their complaints is a minor victory in their battle to retain the use of dividend franking credits for a large group of investors.
The more cynical among them said the two departments have realised how cumbersome the changes will be and want industry help in enforcing the new rules.
Under the franking credit policy, shareholders receive a rebate based on the amount of tax already paid by the company, a measure introduced nine years ago which ended double taxation of dividends.
But the industry does not expect to win significant changes without direct appeals to Treasurer Peter Costello who unexpectedly announced the restrictions in the Federal budget handed down on May 13.

Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) officials met senior Treasury department officers at a dinner last week to discuss the issue, sources said. "We are continuing to liaise with the government," said an ASX spokeswoman, who declined further comment.
The Australian Investment Managers Association (AIMA) also plans to meet the government in the near future.

About 30 submissions from brokers, accountancy firms, and fund managers were sent to the two departments after they held industry meetings in Sydney and Melbourne late last month to explain the changes.
Those who made submissions will be invited to the next meeting in Canberra, a tax department official said.

Many of the submissions argued that the changes were excessive, a case of using a sledgehammer to crack a nut, as the major aim was to end "dividend-washing" schemes where the tax breaks are used by savvy local investors who temporarily buy stock from foreigners who cannot utilise franking credits.

As it now stands, the government has also denied franking credits to any investor who buys and sells a stock within 45 days or who has hedged more than 70 percent of their investment, changes which the industry says threatens equity markets and
Australia's appeal as a reputable capital-raising centre.
AIMA chairman Charles Macek said he had heard that options and derivatives trading was down by up to 30 percent because of the tax changes.

Other brokers and regulators said, however, it is hard to gauge the true impact on derivatives markets as Australian equities are in a boom period and there is little stopping investors at the moment.
"It (the new dividend ruling) comes at a cost but the client is willing to wear the cost rather than run the risk of missing out," said one broker, who asked not to be named.
Macek said the funds management industry will try to show the government that it has made a mistake.

"I think we have a very strong argument to put to a government that is now recognising the importance of tax reform, and indeed that is now beginning to lead the public debate on tax," he told Reuters.

"It seems incongrous that in accepting the need for tax reform they are about to dismantle one of the truly sensible pieces of tax reform that has been initiated in the last 10 years, namely the dividend imputation system."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
